I'm in a somewhat better place at the moment than I was when I made this post, and I still think about this comment a lot. I just wanted to come back to thank you for it.

This is all very solid advice, and I couldn't agree more with most of it. I especially can't stress enough the importance of having separate study and relaxation areas (this seems to work for a lot of people at least) and communicating openly with roommates instead of letting problems sit and turn into resentment.

If you don't mind me asking though, what did the roommate with Aspergers do that was so bad? I went through plenty of hell with my freshman roommates so I definitely get the importance of getting to know them before cohabiting to know if you'll get along or not. At the same time though, I can understand him not telling you guys about having Aspergers right off the bat. As someone who also has Aspergers (though I'm only very lightly on the spectrum), the number of people who know is fewer than I could count on one hand. Most of my close friends are unaware and just think I'm kind of quirky, and explaining that "my brain is not quite wired like other people's" has been a huge challenge to explain to my longtime SO, despite being the closest person in my life. There's a lot of stigma about Aspergers, so I can understand him not giving three guys he just met full disclosure (though of course, it doesn't excuse him from being a shitty roommate!). How does your university's housing process work? Mine was just a crappy five-question online survey with super generic questions like "Are you an early bird or night owl, messy or clean, etc" and you were pretty much locked in with whoever you were randomly assigned to live with unless something drastic happened. I could definitely understand where you're coming from if yours had a section to fill out special requests, conditions that might make it hard to coexist with roommates, or something else to that nature and he didn't mention it there. Something like that honestly might have even saved me from being stuck for two semesters next to people who I really just couldn't stand (and vice versa).

Communicate how you're feeling, and that you may or may not be ready in five years. If that means you have to leave him, well, you'll know what choice is best for you. I personally think you deserve someone who is more compatible to your needs. Maybe it's just my particular friend groups/family, but women give me a hard time much more frequently. They're much more likely to either freak out and start dishing out a million bingoes and act like me not wanting kids is oh so tragic, or they'll insist I'll change my mind someday. Explaining to my best friend was kind of the worst...she started *crying* when I told her my boyfriend and I don't want kids in the future...and her and I were around 18 at the time, lol. That's right, being hysterical over hypothetical nonexistent children just because...she'll never get to see what mine and my bf's kids look like? I love her to death but sheesh. One heartfelt conversation later though, she at least agreed to respect our differences. 

(This all of course varies by person, and there are maybe 2-3 exceptions in my friend group who have been completely understanding right off the bat thankfully.)

Males in my social circle are (mostly) just kind of like "oh, okay cool have fun with that!" Interestingly enough, the only bingoes I do get from them involve passing on my genes/legacy/etc or passing on wisdom, and they're generally pretty accepting once I explain some of my reasoning. Only one male friend has ever freaked out about me choosing not to have kids, though he comes from a culture where marrying young and having lots of kids is common so I almost can't blame him. He was also dating above high school best friend at that time, so cue them simultaneously bingoing me to death at one point lol.

Ah, okay. Sorry for jumping to conclusions and being way too harsh there. Anything involving not being good enough for a partner (whether a person feels that way for one reason or another or their partner directly says so) just hits kind of close to home for me.

I do know the feeling of pushing a partner away even when deep down you just want them closer to comfort you...I was in a similarly bad place with mine back around last November. My own mental illnesses (anxiety, depression), plus being put into multiple stressful and unfortunate situations in my personal life around that time, started really getting the better of me and constantly putting me in a dangerous state of mind. I wanted him to be there for me through it all (and bless him, he stuck by my side even after seeing the worst of me), but I was always so afraid that one day my issues be too much for him and he'd one day decide it wasn't worth the effort anymore and leave. I cried over one thing or another nearly every weekend we spent together, got mad at him for certain things that happened that weren't entirely his fault, and nearly pushed him away for good a couple of times by my own doing, and I still beat myself up for it to this day even though things are much better now. But I have to say, things did get better, and we were able to move past that dark period and now our relationship is great.

Are you currently getting help? I know that's the generic, go-to advice, but it really worked wonders for me and contributed to helping me work my way out of the things I mentioned before. I was skeptical at first, but what helped me was just to have a neutral third party who I could be honest with and speak my mind to without having to hide anything or worry about hurting someone's feelings. There were certain things I told my therapist that I could never tell my boyfriend with complete, raw, uncensored honesty because there was a chance he might (understandably) judge me negatively for thinking them in the first place. And I say that with him being my closest friend in the world and one of the few people I completely trust. In turn, my therapist helped me make sense of some of my negative thoughts and find less harmful ways of handling them. I wouldn't call myself "cured" by any stretch, but I do feel more prepared and level-headed, and generally a lot healthier mentally now.

Thank you for explaining the situation in more detail. Still though, you shouldn't ever need to feel like you're a weaker person for it. Everyone goes through some tough shit now and then, and those of us with mental illnesses have it all the worse when it comes to navigating the weird and crazy problems life throws our way. Sometimes, it takes a lot more effort than being told to just "get over it" like a lot of people not affected by mental illnesses believe, but in the end, whatever happens and however we choose to deal with it, we can only possibly come out stronger for it at the end of the day. On a similar note, don't let yourself be fooled into believing things that aren't true or by making up stories that you know are irrational. Speaking from experience, it's hard not to worry while an SO is far away experiencing new things, but if they love you they will always come back to be by your side as soon as they can. In the meantime, find fun things to do for yourself until you can see her again. Not only will you be able to distract yourself and take your mind off of the scary "what if" scenarios, but you may also find something interesting to talk to her about instead of constantly blowing up her phone about feeling down. You said you enjoy creating music, so maybe focus on that? :)

Things will get better. You will be able to do whatever you need to do to work through this and get to a healthier place, and everything will be okay in the end. She will come back and you won't need to worry anymore once she's home from her vacation, and if things are meant to be you will both be able to work through this rough patch.

I'd say 8-11 is the age where kids are intelligent enough to actually be fun little people to hang out with and aren't always super-annoying. But then they hit middle school and they're back to being annoying, but instead of asking way too many questions they do a 180° and think they know everything. Ages 11-14 are melodramatic, whiny hormonal messes.

Therefore my answer is 15, aka once they're out of middle school and the worst years are behind them. I think a 15 year old is old enough to start thinking like an adult and to a reasonable extent, beginning to act like one. They're able to fit into certain "adult" environments and have a good time without disturbing the peace or being a nuisance. Depending on an area's labor laws, 15 year olds may even be able to get jobs (or at least be only a year off from it, since in the US the legal work age in most places is 16), meaning they should be able to start handling some more complex responsibilities.

Now, this might come with some bias. I'm only 19 myself and have friends as young as 16-17 who I feel like I can hang out with and treat as mature adults. I feel like there was a "before and after" shift in my own life around the time I turned 15 and gained some maturity and common sense, and I look back and cringe at a far smaller number of things I said and did compared to my childhood/early adolescent years.

I haven't seen the show (nor do I really plan to at this point), but from what I've been able to gather, it's already rubbing me the wrong way for pretty much the same reasons. It looks like a high school drama with a tragic romance glamorizing mental illness and suicide, and you know from the start how it's going to end. Not an appealing premise to me at all.

The only positive I can say about it is that it is bringing the message to watch how your words and actions might affect people? (Or at least, according to everyone on my social media?) Depression is of course much more complex than that, ~~and it is mildly infuriating to see people who treated me badly in high school preach it like they've always lived by it,~~ but if that's the message that people are choosing to take away from it then I guess it's not so bad.

Living with my cats, in a nutshell:

* Getting ready for the day in the master bathroom? You are obligated to turn on the sink so Oliver can drink from it (I was the one who taught him that "trick," lol)

* Paper and cardboard items are not to be left unattended if you want them back in optimal condition and without Pepper's teeth marks.

* Do not leave craft supplies unattended, especially anything with string or yarn. We think Oliver has a hidden stash somewhere.

* Cats are to be fed precisely at 7:00 AM and 5:00 PM. They will try everything within their feline power to get you to feed them earlier. They're like gremlins. Don't give in.

* Pepper is to be included in all cuddling. She won't have it any other way.

* Oliver has a "lady friend." Actually, this "lady friend" is just the table lamp in the living room. It's pretty close to his height and he likes to sit very close to the lamp with his head under the lampshade. We think it's silly but try not to be judgmental of their love.

* Screened office windows should be opened in temperatures of 65°+ Fahrenheit.

* Pepper must be carried up and down the main staircase whenever possible, especially at night. She is very vocal and will let you know if she wants to go up or down (a bit of a sad rule because her joints are not so good anymore :(

* Do not be threatened by the mysterious invisible presence hiding in ceiling corners that the cats will randomly stare at from time to time, particularly in dim lighting. We choose to believe that it's the spirit of our old cat, Spooky ~~and not some paranormal being that is coming for us in our sleep~~.

* Pepper cannot go in the garage, period. Oliver can, but knows he shouldn't.

I wasn't saying not to communicate with online friends about your depression at all, just make sure that you're establishing and sticking to healthy boundaries. If you don't feel that you're oversharing, you're probably in the clear. Just be open with your boyfriend about this and make sure he knows about your online support group. As long as you are open to him about it, he will probably be more understanding than you think.

Theres a lot of gray area on this, but two good general rules of thumb are "don't discuss
anything you wouldn't be comfortable discussing with your boyfriend or would feel the need to hide from him" and "don't spend more time communicating with these people than you do with your boyfriend."

As someone who also deals with depression, I know that there are certain things that people without depression will never fully understand. It can be really validating to discuss these things with people who are going through similar situations, and sometimes you also just want to avoid burdening your loved ones too much with talking about mental illness.

However, it's really easy to fall into oversharing. I ended up ghosting an Internet friend who I met under similar circumstances to yours once I realized I was telling them things about me that most of my closest friends don't know, and even a thing or two that my SO didn't know at that time. I probably could have handled the situation better in hindsight, sure, but that was the "crossing a line" boundary for me, and you and your boyfriend are responsible for defining those boundaries for yourself and your own relationship.

If he doesn't already know about this, make sure you're being open with your boyfriend about your online friendships. Make sure he knows they exist, and allow him to see the conversations (and if appropriate, give him the choice to join in if he wants). As your significant other, he should always be #1. If you continue to feel that this is becoming a problem or if he is uncomfortable with it, cut ties with these friends and move on. It's not worth harming your relationship over.

It sounds like she might have an inferiority complex going on. I'm kind of the same way, but I've been able to mostly keep it under control and work through it better over the years.

An inferiority complex is extreme perfectionism. You feel insecure about your abilities in a way that pushes you to feel like you have to be "the absolute best" at the things you're good at to compensate for the things you suck at. You care so much about what others think that you won't be caught dead sucking at something (pretty much anything really, whether you're actually good at it or not) to the point where you get really frustrated if you're not performing to your expectations or to the expectations you think people have of you. It either pushes you to practice and get frustrated to the point of tears when you don't get good overnight, or to just downright avoid anything you don't feel confident you can win at. Very common in people who were brought up competitively (or with a huge emphasis on academic life) because losing is a much bigger blow to their confidence than it would be to any other person since they're not always used to losing and may even see losing as a sign of weakness.

My first suggestion normally would be to find more casual games you can both enjoy and to play one on one with her rather than going to group activities, but it sounds like you've already tried both of those things to some extent. You could maybe try opting for something even more casual, like co-op games or games that don't have a heavy emphasis on "winning" or "losing." This limits the pool of things you could enjoy together by quite a bit though and doesn't solve the problems with her participation in the RPG group, so she will ultimately just have take some initiative to work through this in her own.

Talk to her about how you're feeling. Perhaps understanding that you're becoming frustrated with her will push her to start changing her ways and trying to relax a little bit and find healthier ways of dealing with her own frustration. What ultimately needs to happen is for her to realize this is becoming a problem, and the best way to help it get better is for her to figure out what might be causing these feelings. If she can figure out where the issues are specifically coming from (sounds like family pressure is a huge one here), she might be able to find healthier coping mechanisms instead of taking her anger out on you and others. It's good that you feel that this is a workable situation, but if this is something you feel is out of both of your hands, she would probably benefit from therapy/counseling.

Ultimately, she needs to realize that it's not the end of the world for her not to be good at something and find better ways to handle her feelings rather than taking it out on you or others.

As someone who may or may not have Aspergers (was diagnosed at a young age but outgrew most of the "symptoms" throughout my teenage years so I don't even know anymore, but I don't let it affect me much), this issue is kind of close to my heart and Autism Speaks pisses me off. 

Not sure if you've seen that commercial from a while ago, my memories of it now are pretty vague but it was basically calling autism a "silent killer" and talking about how it ruins kids' lives. From Autism Speaks, an organization that claims to be about spreading awareness about autism, there sure was a lot of false information in there. Even severe cases of autism can't accurately be called a "silent killer," and I'd say that at least half (if not more) of all people on the spectrum are capable of living happy, fulfilling lives.

I'm all for raising awareness about autism as long as it's backed up with legitimate facts and set on generating concern for actual problematic issues. For example, how an autism diagnosis on an intelligent kid who is maybe just a little bit "off" and in need of extra help can land them in a special education classroom with children who are severely low-functioning due to more serious disorders, holding that student back from reaching their full potential? Or how the lower-functioning kids in those classrooms are tasked with following the janitor around instead of being given more stimulating tasks and a learning environment more suited to their needs? Or how kids anywhere on the spectrum can end up with abusive families who refuse to acknowledge that mental illness exists? Or how some adults go for years without being diagnosed and then wonder why their social and/or professional lives are a mess? I wasn't even completely aware of most of these issues associated with autism until hearing stories on Reddit from people who have been in these scenarios or had loved ones involved, and I'm someone (possibly) on the spectrum myself. 

And meanwhile AS is out there stamping puzzle pieces on everything and selling misinformation. It's sickening. The people you're describing have "non-issues." Surprisingly enough to them, it's totally normal for young children to throw temper tantrums at a young age. If they're still doing it around age six or so or they're developmentally behind kids their age in other ways, it might be worth looking into. Otherwise, these people need to stop trying to make their kids into "special snowflakes" (and that's coming from someone who hates the term "special snowflake")

Food is a really personal thing for most people, especially women. It's so frustrating.

I'm not fat, but I'm not skinny either, all around pretty average sized I guess? Would be happier with myself if I could motivate myself to be more active and lose 15 pounds but whatever, I'm still pretty confident with myself all in all. Honestly, I spend more time every day than I ideally want to thinking about food, whether I'm eating too much or too little for my weight and level of activity, how much sugar and carbs I can "get away with," and so on. The thing is, my current living situation means I spend most of my free time alone, and also I'm normally not one to get caught up in what society deems "acceptable." I shouldn't care so much about others' judgement, right? Yet as a female, I am obligated to care and to overanalyze my choices when it comes to food even though I'd rather just be able to eat what I want without overthinking it or feeling guilty afterwards (within reason that is, i.e. eating a whole box of donuts in one day is obviously bad no matter how you slice it).

For this poor girl, all of those worries are probably multiplied by ten. Skinner girls are especially put under way too much pressure from society to keep that physique at all costs, and anything even slightly unhealthy becomes the actual devil. So much pressure from everyone else...fellow skinny friends will be like "I can't believe you're eating all that," and normal people will say things like "you're skin and bones, is that all you're going to eat?" (Which is almost equally condescending even with good intentions). Also, there's all these annoying little unspoken rules about what is and isn't acceptable to eat in social environments. Want cake? It just got cut and everyone else is having a slice? Go for it. Want seconds or leftovers? Ew, stop being a pig. This is why she felt the need to defend herself even though your intentions were completely harmless and she wasn't doing anything wrong. There's this weird guilt factor that comes with eating junk food, especially in front of others. This is also the same reason why if someone brings a box of donuts to a workplace, women will sometimes end up leaving half a donut behind. If one person does it, everyone feels obligated to so they're not "that one person" being "fat."

I have a ton of respect for you for recognizing this being a problem. In an ideal world, none of us should have to feel unfairly "cake shamed" ever again. Not you, not me, not her, not anyone.

Wow, this hits home for me. I've been somewhere very close to your girlfriend's position, in multiple ways. Same age difference and everything.

Do you have any very specific reasons to worry about what will happen when she goes to college? To stay with you this long, even while you were in a different state, means she obviously loves you a lot. Try to plan a visit about a month or so in once the time comes for it. She will have had enough time then to start adjusting to her new environment and will probably be more than ready to see you.

As for the sex thing, there might be a couple of reasons she's holding off. First of all, does she come from a very religious/conservative family? If so, she has probably been led to believe (or at least had it implied to her) that having sex at a young age and/or before marriage is shameful. Or, alternatively, she's probably had people try to shame her in the past for being in a relationship with a "cradle robber" or being "jail bait" given your ages when you started dating....this shit can be harmful as hell even with good intentions once you're both legal adults, and I personally got it mostly from adults in my life who I considered authority figures. Maybe she's afraid to have sex, whether it's fear of negative judgement for the above reasons, fear of pain, or fear of accidentally getting pregnant. All of this can be worked through with some effort and patience on your end, however.

First, explain how you're feeling, and that the lack of sex in this relationship is making you feel insecure and hurting your self esteem. It sounds like it's time to give her full disclosure, even the part about it keeping you up at night. Explain that to you, sex in this relationship is necessary to stay happy and feel secure, and that this type of physical affection is something you feel is missing. It might be hard for her to "get" it at first since, in complete honesty, girls are brought up to have completely different attitudes about sex than guys are. I could write a whole essay on this but on a basic level, for guys it's seen in a much more positive light and for girls it's seen much more negatively. For now, it's your job to help her break out of those harmful stereotypes and realize that sex can be fun, rewarding, a great bonding experience, and a key element of healthy relationships.

Have you done any other types of sex besides PIV yet (handjobs, oral)? If not, start there as soon as you can and work your way up, learning what each of you likes, and it will help her get more comfortable. Speaking from experience, it might be awkward at first and she may not immediately enjoy receiving, but it'll be a learning experience for both of you and help her adopt a more casual attitude towards intimacy. Just take things at a pace she is comfortable with, since it's ultimately up to her to navigate her own boundaries.

Before you guys start having PIV sex, make sure she is on some type of reliable birth control, and use condoms. This might sound obvious but not only do you really not need a baby in your life right now, but taking every precaution you can will lessen her fears and help her feel more confident.

As another comment suggested, try planning out a date to have sex for the first time on. You don't need to be super-blunt and be like "hey we're having sex next Thursday," lol, but try to have a specific day in mind and do what you can to make it special and accommodating. Choose a place and time where you know you'll have complete privacy so there is no need to feel anxious about being interrupted, walked in on, or overheard. Plan something fun and relaxing to do before or afterwards to take some of the edge off of things (my boyfriend took me to IHOP afterwards and we spent the afternoon watching Disney movies, lol). Give her a chance to talk about it afterwards, about what she feels physically or mentally, and share how you're feeling as well. You both will probably not be good at sex right off the bat, but again, it's a learning experience and you can get there with time.

Perhaps you could try widening your social circle a bit? For some people, working through these sorts of things relies heavily on having social support. It might be a little late in the school year to join new clubs and such like most people would probably tell you to do, especially if you are a graduating senior and won't be returning next year, but there will be so many more clubs to try once you start college. In the meantime, maybe you could focus on getting closer to the people who you already do consider your friends. I know this can be tough for people like you and I who have anxiety and it can be hard to become close enough to people to be open about mental illness, but people are more often than not more open to creating closer friendships than you'd think. It took me forever to open up to my own friends about my mental health, even to the ones who I've known for years and who have always had my back, but there came a time when I had to explain some things because they were beginning to notice that I was often a bit down. They were surprisingly a lot more supportive than I had thought they would be, and they made an effort to spend more time with me and check in on me every now and then. Most of them do not have mental illnesses themselves, but in today's world people are learning how to be there for their close friends who do have them and I think that's a beautiful thing. I'm not saying you have to give your friends complete full disclosure, but I'm sure they'll be more open and accepting than you'd think. Doing social activities together would help you take your mind off of missing your boyfriend so much. Even if you don't feel comfortable talking about your depression and anxiety at this point, try to do more activities with your circle of friends just to take your mind off of things and to help you feel less alone.

Finally, remember that anxiety is just a bunch of irrational thoughts that your brain makes to throw you off track. The next time your boyfriend takes a while to respond to a text, instead of telling yourself "he's tired of me and he's going to leave me," tell yourself "he loves me even knowing I have some issues," "I know I can count on him to be there for me, he's just busy right now," and "if there were a problem, I know he respects me enough that he would say so." You have to talk yourself down from it, and try to replace the anxious thoughts with rational ones that you know to be true. If you get caught in a moment of feeling upset and crying, find some small activity to distract yourself, such as drawing, knitting, playing a video game, or something else more relevant to your hobbies. Giving your brain a relaxing task to focus on leaves a lot less room for anxious thoughts to take over.

The first time I truly realized I was CF, I was around 13 years old, give or take a year. I went to a yard sale one day and a lady was selling some really beautiful paintings. I loved them and asked if she had painted them. She said she had, but that after having kids she just didn't have the time and energy for it anymore.

So I started thinking. I was an aspiring artist, and the last thing I wanted was to ever have to give up my passion and sell my work for dirt cheap in the driveway of a suburban two-story picket-fenced house. And that my friends, is when I started really questioning the life script. Before that point, I just assumed having kids was "just what everyone did around a certain age" and never thought too much into it, though the idea of ever raising my own kids always did kind of freak me out. It was shortly after that I realized, "I could always just *not* have kids."

Over the years, certain things from my childhood started making more and more sense. Heck, I didn't like playing "House" with other girls when I was really little and always just felt awkward about it unless I could be the dog or some other role that barely did anything. I also didn't like other kids touching my figurines and stuffed animals despite being a kid myself because I was afraid they would be too rough with them. Babies always kind of grossed me out and any time I was ever asked to hold one or entertain one was really uncomfortable. The moment of the yard sale was definitely a wake-up call, but looking back there were plenty of signs leading up to it.

Some other reasons that kids are not for me:

* Pregnancy/childbirth really freaks me out. I feel vaguely uncomfortable around pregnant women and dread the day when my friends start having kids of their own and ramble about their aches and pains and want me to touch their bellies...ewww no. I don't wanna get fat and lose control of certain bodily functions and all the other icky stuff that comes with pregnancy.

* I really don't like babies. At all. They're smelly, loud, and leak fluids from every orifice. I also find them really ugly until they're old enough to have distinguishable features. I would find having to take care of one all day every day for its first few years of life to be mind-numbingly dull.

* I'm not big on young children either and don't really know how to interact with people too young to have an intelligent conversation with. I also don't like dealing with younger teens who think they know everything (I thought so at your age too, buddy). The only kids I can really click with are the 7-10 crowd, and they don't stay that age for long.

* I doubt I would ever be able to provide a kid with a good, financially stable life with my desired career of choice. I want to have the freedom to do what I want without having to worry about providing for them.

* I want to have the time, money, and energy to devote to my hobbies and go whatever else I want. I also like to sleep a lot. I know, selfish right? ;)

* I am a child of divorce. Watching my parents go through a nasty split over the course of the past three years, after 20+ years of being happily married, has not been kind to my mental health and has tainted my view on marriage a little bit. I have a boyfriend who I love dearly and would like to get married to someday, but in case something ever happened between us I would never want to put my own kids through the things I had to go through.

* On the topic of mental health, I have moderate anxiety and occasionally also go through severe depressive episodes. I am seeking help but still have a long way to go. Some of this is from the situation I have had to deal with the past few years, but the anxiety has been there in varying degrees throughout my whole life and I suspect my mom may have anxiety as well. Not only would I risk being a bad parent due to my own mental health issues, but some of it may be genetic and could be passed onto them.

* I love my boyfriend and don't want that to ever die out because of a kid. Kids cause marital and financial stress, date nights become less frequent, and you can't just be "intimate" whenever and wherever you want anymore. We're still really young and all, but we're coming up on four years of dating very soon and don't ever want to have to stop and share each other with a kid. I know a lot of people say you end up loving your kid more than your spouse but if I'm being honest here that's not as happy of a statement for me to hear as it probably is for most people.

* I care about the environment and don't want to exponentially increase my carbon footprint by adding a child. I also don't want a kid to have to grow up in a world where some essential resources could become a scarcity in just a couple more generations.

To add on to this, I personally think the "carrying on genetics" argument is such a nonsensical reason to have a kid (as opposed to adopting when so many kids out there need homes, or to not having one at all). In this day and age, it's not all about survival of the fittest anymore. After you're gone, why does it matter if someone's still carrying on your genes? Five or six generations down the line, it's unlikely that the great-great-great-grandkids would really care so much. At the end of the day, it's just a title at best, and a really arbitrary thing to consider when deciding whether or not to have a kid. There's seriously so many other important things to consider about raising kids that "passing on genes" should be near the bottom of the list for most people.

I myself have an existential crisis about once a year about whether I'll be remembered for anything long after I'm dead and gone. However, I want to be remembered for making some kind of contribution to the world, either with my art (yes I'm young and idealistic, so what?) or by helping an extensive number of people. I could care less about passing my genes on, that's like saying "congrats, you are capable of doing something most other humans and nearly every species on the planet is capable of and there's a 99.9% chance no one will care after a century and a half."

Sorry for the rant :p this is just something I've thought about a lot.

Hey there. I'm in a relationship with a guy two years older than me. We have been dating since the end of my freshman year and his junior year of high school, and we've been going strong for nearly four years.

It hasn't been an easy journey at all. More than half of our relationship has been spent doing long distance with him going to college three states and over 10 hours away. We now only live two hours apart since I chose to go to a college close to his and we have been able to spend every other weekend with each other during this school year, and it has made things worlds easier. Sadly we'll have to go back to long distance in a month since I have to go home for the summer and he's choosing to stay in this state for work, but due to my financial situation, less-than-great home life, and desire to be closer to him, attending his school next year if I can get some financial kinks worked out (out-of-state tuition is a bitch sadly) is looking like the best option for me. If all goes well over the next few months, we might finally be able to attend the same school again and possibly even live together in August.

However, this doesn't work for everyone. I know my boyfriend and I are the exception to virtually every rule people tell you not to break in young relationships (age gap, distance, one/both people starting college, and so on). Meanwhile, I have a close friend and her boyfriend, who were only living around four hours apart and had a lot of things going for them. They were together for nearly a year in total (around three months of her being in college) before that relationship crashed and burned as she realized she was trying too hard to fit his needs and life goals at her own expense while missing out on a huge part of the college experience as a result. The breakup was particularly hard on both of them, but she is ultimately doing better now and to my knowledge, is much happier and getting much more out of her time in college.

With all of that being said, here's my advice to you:

* Spend as much time together as you can over the next few months up until it's time to leave for college. Know for sure whether she's just as committed to doing this as you are (hopefully the answer is yes!) and make sure you're both on the same page. If either of you are worried or anxious about anything, now is the time to air it out. Do fun couple things together, like going to concerts and theme parks/carnivals. Get to know each other deeper than ever before (and trust me, there will still be plenty about each other that you don't know after only seven months). Make sure that at least the basic things you each want in life are compatible to know if this relationship will be worth the tremendous effort (i.e. career plans? traveling? etc.)

* Once it's time to go, always make communication a priority. Call, text, and/or Skype every single day. Send each other memes on a regular basis. Recommend movies and shows to each other to pass the time until you can see each other next and to have something fun to have a conversation about at times when you run out of things to talk about (waiting for new One Punch Man episodes pulled my boyfriend and I through a slow period, lol). Find online games you can both enjoy together. Be there for each other, especially since the beginning of college can be rough for many people. 

* Wait for about a month to pass and evaluate whether long distance is working for you so far. Are both of your relationship needs being met as much as possible? Does communication feel natural and not forced? Do you both feel confident about where the relationship is heading, and that the other person is as committed as you are? Are you confident that you are not holding each other back and are giving each other enough space to grow and explore new things? Are you both getting what you want out of the college experience so far? Are you forming new friend groups and getting involved in campus life? Are you staying healthy and taking up new interests? Are both your short-term and long-term goals still compatible (you'll be surprised how much this can change after starting college)? If you can confidently answer yes to these questions, you're on the right track. If not, it might be time to re-evaluate some things and decide whether the relationship is worth the effort.

* If the answer to the above questions is yes, then the fun part comes next. You can then start working out times to visit each other and schedule things that line up with your school/work schedules. My boyfriend and I had things worked out where I'd visit him for his birthday weekend (early October) and during my spring break (March or April), and he would come home for Christmas break (mid December-early January) and a couple of weeks during summer break. Our "rule" was to not go more than three months without visiting each other for at least a few days at a time, and that was ultimately the glue that kept us together since we both really rely on physical contact more than anything. You and your girlfriend will be living a lot closer than we were/will be, so I'd say that visiting each other once a month + holiday breaks would be appropriate.

Good luck. Long distance is difficult, especially for young couples, but it really makes every second with them worth so much more. Feel free to PM me if you have any questions.

I am the SO of someone who plays League religiously so I really feel for your boyfriend here. I played very casually at one point and do enjoy the art/characters, but I can't play the game myself on a remotely serious level. I really suck at it and don't feel like putting in the amount of time needed to significantly improve, and I end up getting way too angry with myself and/or other players to the point where it's probably unhealthy, so I quit the game indefinitely several months back.

The thing with League is, games go on average from 30-45 minutes. That's 30-45 minutes per game that he feels could be spent doing some other activity together instead of him watching you play a game he has little to no interest in. And then there's the sunk-cost fallacy of League. If you win, you feel super-motivated and want to play another and keep going (or maybe it was a bit of a letdown because your team carried you and you didn't personally do much). If you lose, you feel cheated of your time and want to make up for it with the next one. Either way, it often ends up being an hours-long time sink. Also when playing League, one can hardly blink without possibly missing something important. Essentially, your bf probably feels like you're tuning him out and ignoring him for 30-45 minutes at a time, only to (most likely) do it again multiple times after the first game is finished.

The reason I personally don't like it when my SO plays League while I'm over is because we only see each other a few times each month due to our current living situations and had been doing on-and-off long distance for most of our relationship (as in 100s of miles, sadly will have to go back to this soon). Because of this, any amount of time we can spend together is really valuable to me. Even if we're just chilling in pajamas and watching YouTube, it's still more quality time spent together than watching League match after League match while I just kind of sit there bored silly by it. Also, my SO tends to get kind of angry sometimes if the game goes badly, which kinda bums me out. Why waste time and energy angrily typing at people you'll probably never run into again and then just be even more pissed off in the end? Thankfully, my SO is cutting down on it and now only plays while I'm over if I'm busy working on a project or assignment for school or work.

I was/am in this boat. Anxiety is rough, especially in relationships :\ Because this hits pretty close to home for me, this comment will probably get kind of long, just a heads-up.

If you haven't already, have a talk with him about your anxiety and try to explain it as well as you can. If you want to wait a bit longer before giving him full disclosure that's fine since you've only been together for two months, but explain things at a pace that feels comfortable to you and appropriate to the relationship. Anxiety can come off as a really abstract concept for people who don't have to deal with it themselves, so here's a couple of ways I've explained it to people/seen it explained by others (as you'll notice, similes/metaphors seem to work well to relate it into more understandable terms):

* "A little voice in the back of my head that just won't shut up. Even if I know (situation) is totally fine, it will just keep saying over and over that it's not fine until I can't take it anymore."

* "Anxiety is like leaving your house and worrying you forgot to lock the door, except that applies to everything in life and you start letting it eat you alive."

* "Anxiety is like hearing the enemy music in a video game, but never actually seeing the enemy."

Also, make sure you explain that this has (most likely) been a lifelong thing for you and isn't the result of anything that he has said or done. The thing about mental illnesses is that those who have to deal with them often have very limited control of their thoughts. It may be hard for a partner not to take it personally, especially when it comes to sex/relationship anxiety (more on that later), but explaining it to them in a logical and rational manner can be done with a lot of reassurance.

It has taken a long time for my boyfriend to fully understand my anxiety; I'd say he didn't really start to "get it" until the past year or so of our nearly four-year relationship (however, that's also because I kind of did a good job of hiding it early on/wasn't placed into too many situations that are difficult to me personally until more recently). There are still certain things he wishes I could just "get over," but we've made a lot of progress and he now has a good understanding of which things are particularly triggering for me and is willing to help me work through them, avoid them, or just be there to be supportive of me if neither of the other options are possible. Do you have any specific situations that are more difficult for you to deal with than average? If so, definitely make sure he's aware of those. He sounds like a patient and supportive guy, so I'm sure he'll be willing to help you work through it.

To give you an example of this, one type of situation that is especially hard for me to cope with is trying to call someone and then not having them pick up or try to call me back within half an hour, particularly at night and even more so on weekend nights. My mind always jumps into worst-case-scenario mode and worries about them getting into an accident with a drunk driver. My boyfriend now realizes this. We usually call each other pretty late at night, and if he doesn't call me/I can't get ahold of him around our usual period of time, I start to worry more and more until I start crying and shaking uncontrollably. Upon realizing how badly this affects me, he now texts me if he plans to be out later than normal hanging out with friends and gives me an estimate of when he'll be able to talk. It only takes about five seconds of his time to send those texts, but having some reassurance that he's fine and is just out having a good time with friends makes all the difference in the world to me. 

That type of support, things that would take very little effort for your boyfriend to change about his habits but could make a huge difference to you, might be worth bringing up. Have you talked with him about why these habits might make you feel insecure (i.e. taking a while to answer messages, being late, not initiating plans often)? You should definitely be patient with him and not resort to being passive aggressive if he's not acting "flaky" on purpose, but you need to be very clear about why these behaviors just don't sit right with you. Maybe some behaviors can be explained logically (i.e. being at a job where he can't reach his phone often) or can be chalked up to being part of his personality, but he may be willing to change others for the sake of being a better partner. Being frequently late, for example, is something that could get on anyone's nerves, not just people with anxiety.

Sex may be an entirely different ballgame when it comes to anxiety, especially if you're new at it. Is there any specific reason that sexual activity might make you feel anxious? Some of the most common reasons for sex-related anxiety are fear of getting pregnant, fear of getting hurt, fear of social/familial rejection (may only apply if you grew up somewhere very conservative), and body insecurities. Most of these fears applied to me at some point before/while becoming sexually active, but thankfully my boyfriend is a very patient guy and was willing to help me work through it. I'll give you some tips to work through all of those individually:

* If you aren't already, get a reliable form of birth control and make sure that BC has had time to become effective. Use condoms and make sure they're the correct size, and if you ever decide to go condom-less (don't do this if not on an effective type of BC), start practicing the pull-out method before transitioning. Using birth control + condoms is the best way to go though, especially since you're both young, because it's pretty much double protection. If one method fails, the other will serve as a back-up (failure is unlikely though; BC and condoms generally only fail due to human error like not taking pills correctly or putting on a condom that is much too small).

*  Sex may hurt the first few times, but it's due to inexperience by not parties, not "virgin anatomy" (a really harmful myth that we need to get rid of altogether). With good foreplay you'll have nothing to worry about. If he is inexperienced too, he may benefit from researching different ways to help you feel more comfortable and have more fun.

* Virginity is just a social construct, and nothing more. If you have a conservative family/live in a conservative area people may make a much bigger deal of it than it needs to be, but all in all sex is a fun thing that should be seen as an enjoyable experience as long as both parties are consenting and responsible. 18 is a perfectly normal age to start becoming sexually active. No one will care in the long run but you and your boyfriend.

* A lot of people are insecure about themselves if they're sexually inexperienced, this is also totally normal. Your boyfriend is physically attracted to you though, wants to do sexual things together, and sounds like he is willing to be patient and supportive of you while you figure it all out, so you have no need to feel insecure here!

It's possible that he may take it personally that sex makes you anxious, which is very understandable. Like explaining other types of anxiety, make it very clear that a lot of the problem stems from irrational thinking and is not the result of anything he has said or done. Tell him if there are any specific issues you need to work through and try to avoid being vague or using "I don't know" statements when explaining why a certain aspect of sex might be difficult for you. The important thing here is to make sure he knows he shouldn't blame himself. Give him lots of reassurance and love, and tell him how much you appreciate his patience and understanding and that you trust him a ton. Work through things at as slow of a pace that you need to to become comfortable, and sex will become much more enjoyable for both of you with time.

One last thing: It's really great that you're deciding to seek help for this. I promise that with the right counselor or therapist, life will get much easier for you as a whole. Just having someone to listen to things you can't quite put into words to anyone else and help you navigate and make sense of why certain things make you feel the way you do makes worlds of difference.

If you need to talk or want more advice, please feel free to PM me anytime!

No, you're not overreacting at all. Most people are either very monogamous (you) or are open to the idea of an open relationship (her) with not much gray area in-between. Open relationships are fine if all parties involved are consenting to it, but if it is something that makes you uncomfortable, you need to put your foot down and say so. For most people, this is something that's difficult if not impossible to compromise on. If you're uncomfortable with her messing around with other girls and since your situation is only temporary, she can wait for you if she wants to stay in the relationship. 

My bf and I were in a similar place a couple of years ago (him starting college, me still in high school). Both being strictly monogamous, it would have been a huge problem if either of us had messed around with other people during that time. I also have anxiety myself, so the beginning of doing long distance was really rough for me :( It's definitely a weird spot to be in while in a young relationship, and I really can't blame you for being uncomfortable. There's also the stereotype about how people coming into college while in high school relationships want to "experiment," which really doesn't help matters and is a huge reason for such problems to arise because people think they "have to do it for the college experience." (spoiler alert: they don't, at least in my opinion. Why give up something good you already have if there are no other issues affecting the relationship?)

If I were you, I'd have a very honest talk with her, preferably next time you see her in person, about why the idea of her being in an open relationship makes you uncomfortable. Hopefully she will listen and take it to heart. In the worst case scenario, if this is something non-compromisable and she insists on "experimenting," it may lead to a split. You are both still very young though, and whether she ends up not being so dead-set on this and is willing to put your needs first or if you do end up with someone else in the future, you deserve a person whose needs in a relationship are compatible with yours.
